strengths: A clearly written paper with sound results.
The introduction of the problem is a nice conceptual contribution.
The new algorithm they proposed could also have other applications.
In the notion of a "natural algorithm" is a nice contribution since it allows the analysis of algorithms and lower bounds.
The studied problem is well-motivated, both from the literature review on incremental learning, and from empirical estimation.
The theoretical analysis is complete, an upper bound and lower bound is provided for this problem, as well as compared to state of the art as in table 1.
The logic of this paper is easy to follow, and the assumptions/notations are presented in a clear way.
The paper has additional experiments on the ridge regression problem.

Originality: the setting is interesting, and the proposed algorithm is novel as far as I know. In their algorithm, they propose to switch between compute full gradient with i FOs and compute a simple modification based on the previous gradient with 1 FO for full gradient estimation, which is a special trick.
Quality: The results are nice, because the authors not only provide the convergence guarantees, but also compare it with the existing methods, and provide a very close lower bound.
Clarity: The overall writing of this paper is excellent.
Significance: I think the results are interesting, because this setting is an important setting to explore, and they have presented a full story about this setting.
weaknesses: I can’t connect Problem 2 with its motivation; I don’t see a motivation for the problem.

You give lower bounds only for natural algorithms; it is unclear why only natural algorithms are considered and a simple algorithm could achieve an O(log n / ε) bound that outperforms all suggested methods.
Experiments are only conducted in simple regression settings; dataset statistics (e.g. the number of points) are not shown and it is unclear how exactly you execute the baselines.
Commas are missing in many places.
You mention O(n \log \frac{1}{\epsilon}) complexity for VR methods, but the same bound is achievable by trivial deterministic gradient descent by sampling all n functions at every iteration.
Page 2: “for Problem 1 using O(1/\epsilon)”. – “FOs” is missing.
A weakness is the lack of intuition about their algorithm; conceptually it is unclear why the algorithm obtains an improvement in the epsilon power.
In the experiments, the authors analyze a version of ridge regression where they divide by i for every step, which seems unnatural and may artificially harden the problem.
The authors do not list the parameters of the dataset and the ε used in the algorithm.
The upper bound provided by the algorithm is not tight compared to the lower bound.
The algorithm only works in the strongly convex case.
There is no input in algorithm 2.
The value of α needs to be in line 2 of algorithm 1.
Additional "the" in the second line of the first paragraph of section 3.1.
The VR is never defined; a suggestion is to define "variance reduction (VR)" and then use VR afterwards.

The main weakness is the strong convexity assumption of f, which is considered outdated for modern deep neural network models, and variance reduced techniques may not be useful for neural networks, making the proposed method less practical for real‑world models.
